slides.title: Background and motivation
slides.heading: Background and motivation
slides.subtitle: Why hybrid, lightweight and explainable Android malware detection matters
slides.review_note: Motivation prose is not copied from a thesis PDF in this workspace. Content below is limited to facts evidenced by the executed notebooks and local datasets.
bullets: Android malware research commonly combines static and dynamic signals; this project evaluates API-call sequences, system-call frequencies and network-flow tables as separate modalities.
The executed final ensemble (notebook cell 4) classifies NF-UQ-NIDS network flows — not APK packages directly.
Class imbalance is material: cell-4 flows used 49,414 normal vs 100,586 attack among 150,000 rows; the API file is heavily malware-skewed (≈39.7:1).
Lightweight stacks and resampling were studied to balance detection quality against model size relative to a CNN–BiLSTM benchmark.

notes.main_point: Frame the threat and modality landscape without overstating multimodal fusion.
notes.contribution: Sets up why MI–GA, resampling and lightweight ensembles were studied.

slides.heading: Research problem statement
slides.subtitle: Evidence-aligned problem framing
slides.review_note: A formal thesis problem statement was not found in the workspace. Replace this wording with the approved thesis text before the viva if required.
bullets: Problem observed in the experimental programme: high headline accuracy can coexist with poor specificity under imbalance (cell-22 ADASYN FPR 0.6111).
Problem observed: heavy models (CNN–BiLSTM ≈1.11M parameters) versus lightweight stacks (≈75k parameters in the cell-4 ensemble).
Problem observed: feature selection and resampling choices materially change outcomes; protocols that resample before the split inflate optimism.
Problem observed: API and network rows are not joined by application id in the executed final run — multimodal claims require careful wording.

slides.title: Research findings and contributions
slides.heading: Research findings and contributions
slides.subtitle: Findings supported by verified outputs
bullets: Finding: among cell-4 stacking runs, SMOTE-ENN achieved the highest F1 (0.97789) under the notebook protocol.
Finding: lightweight stacking (75,004 parameters) is far smaller than the CNN–BiLSTM benchmark (1,108,931 parameters).
Finding: resampling that maximises F1 can degrade balanced accuracy and inflate FPR (cell 22).
Finding: a leakage-corrected local retrain remains strong (≈0.9663 accuracy) but is not equivalent to the notebook score.
Finding: executed final ensemble evidence is network-flow based.

slides.title: Limitations, conclusion and future work
slides.heading: Limitations, conclusion and future work
slides.subtitle: Honest boundaries of the current evidence
bullets: Limitation: final executed ensemble scores network flows, not APKs; no paired API+flow id.
Limitation: notebook resample-before-split and in-sample meta-fitting inflate optimism risk.
Limitation: Kaggle weights / LRP JSON / full ROC curves unavailable locally; repeated-run statistics Not established.
Conclusion (evidence-based): AMSEC demonstrates a lightweight stacking pathway with competitive notebook metrics and a working leakage-aware prototype.
Future work (for review with thesis): paired multimodal ids, out-of-fold stacking, exported probability curves, on-device measurement, repeated trials.
